The Latin Fathers
LAT-in FAH-therz
noun (historical, plural)
From Latin, the language of the Western church; father from Latin pater, applied to the early teachers who handed down the apostolic faith.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Latin Fathers were the early Christian writers of the Western, Latin-speaking church, chiefly Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and above all Augustine of Hippo. To them the church owes a great debt under God. Tertullian gave the Latin vocabulary of the Trinity; Ambrose defended the deity of Christ against the Arians and baptized Augustine; Jerome rendered the Scriptures into the Latin Vulgate; and Augustine, the greatest of them, set forth the doctrines of original sin, sovereign grace, and predestination that the Reformers would later prize as their own inheritance. Calvin cited Augustine more than any other father. Yet they were men, not the apostles; and where they erred the church must say so. Their reverence for tradition, their early notions of baptismal regeneration, and their developing views of the church and the sacraments became seedbeds upon which a later Rome built corruptions the apostles never taught. This dictionary honors the Latin Fathers for guarding Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy and for Augustine's doctrine of grace, while measuring all they wrote by the rule of Scripture, the only infallible standard.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early Western theologians—Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and chiefly Augustine—who guarded Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy and, in Augustine, the doctrine of grace. The Reformers honored their contributions while measuring all by Scripture.

THE LATIN FATHERS, noun, plural. The early Christian writers of the Western church, foremost among them Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine.

They defended the Trinity and the deity of Christ, and in Augustine set forth the doctrines of original sin and sovereign grace.

"By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God" (Eph 2:8), the truth Augustine recovered against Pelagius.

Their writings require the reverence due to faithful teachers, yet forbid the place of an infallible rule, which Scripture alone holds.

Their sense in history: a foundation of orthodoxy upon which Rome later raised corruptions the Reformers had to remove.

📖 Key Scripture

Eph 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Rom 5:12 — "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:"

2 Tim 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

Acts 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Rome appeals to the Latin Fathers to underwrite later corruptions; against this the doctrine honors their genuine contributions yet subjects them to Scripture, the sole infallible rule.

expand to see more

Rome appeals to the Latin Fathers to justify doctrines the apostles never taught—the sacrifice of the mass, baptismal regeneration as a settled dogma, prayers for the dead, the swelling authority of the bishop of Rome—as though development from a father's seedling word were equal to the word of God. But the fathers themselves bowed to the Scriptures. Augustine wrote that he gave to the canonical books alone the honor of believing they could not err, and to all others only the deference due to fallible men.

The Reformation was no rejection of the fathers but a return to their own rule. Calvin and the Reformers claimed Augustine's doctrine of grace against the medieval church that had buried it, and read the fathers as helpful servants, never as masters over Scripture. The error is not to value the Latin Fathers but to lift them to an authority they themselves disclaimed.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin, the tongue of the Western church, and the title pater (father) given the early teachers who handed down the faith once delivered.

expand to see more

Tertullian of Carthage, who first wrought the Latin language of the Trinity, trinitas and persona.

Cyprian of Carthage, bishop and martyr, who wrote on the unity of the church.

Ambrose of Milan, who withstood the Arians and instructed the young Augustine.

Jerome, the scholar who translated the Scriptures into the Latin Vulgate.

Augustine of Hippo, doctor of grace, whose Confessions and anti-Pelagian works the Reformers prized.

Usage

"The seminary course on the Latin Fathers began with Tertullian and ended with Augustine."

"He showed how the Reformers claimed the Latin Fathers, especially Augustine, against the church of Rome."

"Reading the Latin Fathers, she learned to honor their wisdom without granting them the authority of Scripture."
